You are reverse-engineering the `codehilite` markdown extension's behavior in the executable /workspace/dataset/test13_executable so it can be reimplemented in JavaScript with ZERO dependencies. Context: the program runs `markdown.markdown(args.b, extensions=['codehilite'])` for the `--b` argument. Run probes like: /workspace/dataset/test13_executable --a 'A' --b $' indented code here' --c 'C' (the `--b` output is the 2nd printed line; `--a`/`--c` are trivial markers). Use $'...' quoting for newlines. Never use the `python` command. We already know: - An indented (4-space) code block in --b renders as: `
...CODE...\n
` - For input ` code_b()` the CODE is plain, with NO tokens. - For input ` def f(x):\n return "s" # c` the CODE contains Pygments token spans with classes nv, w, ss, k, s2 — i.e. Pygments' `guess_lexer` picked SOME lexer (NOT the Python lexer — Python would give `k` for `def` and `nf` for `f`). So `guess_lang` appears to be ON. Pygments' guess_lexer scores every lexer's analyse_text() and raises ClassNotFound when all scores are 0, in which case codehilite falls back to a plain TextLexer (no spans). YOUR MISSION — determine, empirically and precisely: 1. THE BOUNDARY: which indented-code inputs produce NO spans (plain passthrough, the TextLexer path) versus which produce spans. Probe a wide, systematic corpus of one-line and multi-line code blocks: plain English prose; a single word; a number; Chinese text; `x = 1`; `print("hi")`; `def f():`; `function f() {}`; `SELECT * FROM t`; ``; `#!/bin/sh`; `{"a": 1}`; `a:b`; `- item`; `int main(){}`; `class A:`; `if x: pass`; `foo(bar)`; `echo hi`; `x++;`; text with a trailing colon; text with quotes; text with `#` comments; a line with only punctuation; indented blocks of 1, 2, 3 lines. For EACH, report the exact full `--b` output line(s). 2. Characterize WHICH lexer wins for the span-producing cases (infer from the token class names and the way tokens are split), and how stable/predictable it is. Report the exact span markup for each. 3. Determine whether TextLexer output does ANY escaping/transformation: test code containing `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'`, backslashes, tabs, trailing whitespace, blank lines inside the block, and non-ASCII. Report exact bytes (pipe through `| cat -A` when whitespace matters). 4. Determine the exact wrapper markup invariants: is there always exactly `` right after `
`? Is there a newline after ``? Does the code always end with `\n` before ``? Does the div ever get extra attributes? Test a block whose last line has no trailing newline vs one that does.

5. Test the CodeHilite special first-line directives in --b: `#!python` as the first line of an indented block; `:::python` as the first line; `:::text`; `:::nonexistentlang`. Report the exact output for each (does the directive line get removed? does a `class` or `linenums` appear? does it produce `` line numbers?). Also test `#!text` and a shebang like `#!/usr/bin/env python`.

6. Determine whether codehilite affects INLINE code spans (`` `x` ``) or only block code. And confirm what a ``` fenced block does in --b (we believe fenced_code is NOT enabled there, so it becomes an inline code span) — verify with several fence shapes.

7. MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL QUESTION: estimate how likely a JS port is to be wrong. Specifically, determine whether ordinary prose / natural-language text / Chinese text in an indented block ALWAYS takes the no-span TextLexer path. Give a crisp, defensible rule of the form "input X produces plain output; input Y produces spans", listing every span-producing trigger you found, and note which triggers a JS port could reasonably emulate.

Output a dense technical report: exact inputs, exact outputs, and the inferred rules. Do not speculate without labeling it as inference. Run MANY probes — batch several per bash call with echo separators.
